claim: Male germ cells share a common origin across animal species.
source: Male germ cells share a common origin across animal species, therefore they likely retain a conserved genetic program that defines their cellular identity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: The average functional requirement of a metazoan male germ cell corresponds to the expression of approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes.
source: We estimate the average functional requirement of a metazoan male germ cell to correspond to the expression of approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes, a third of which defines a genetic scaffold of deeply conserved genes that has been retained throughout evolution.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis across three species using TPM >1 as a threshold, as shown in Figure 1b and described in the Results section.

claim: A third of the approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes expressed in male germ cells defines a genetic scaffold of deeply conserved genes.
source: We estimate the average functional requirement of a metazoan male germ cell to correspond to the expression of approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes, a third of which defines a genetic scaffold of deeply conserved genes that has been retained throughout evolution.
evidence: This is derived from phylostratigraphy analysis showing 65.2-70.3% of expressed genes map to phylostrata 1-5 (Figure 1d).

claim: The conserved genetic scaffold contains a set of 79 functional associations between 104 gene expression regulators that represent a core component of the conserved genetic program of metazoan spermatogenesis.
source: Such scaffold contains a set of 79 functional associations between 104 gene expression regulators that represent a core component of the conserved genetic program of metazoan spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is derived from orthoBackbone network analysis and GO term enrichment, as shown in Figure 2e.

claim: 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes were uncovered through genetic interference with male germ cell identity.
source: By genetically interfering with the acquisition and maintenance of male germ cell identity, we uncover 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes and three new potential genetic causes of human infertility.
evidence: This is based on in vivo RNAi screening in Drosophila and literature review to determine novelty, as shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Three new potential genetic causes of human infertility were identified: RNF113B, HSPA2, and KPNA2.
source: By genetically interfering with the acquisition and maintenance of male germ cell identity, we uncover 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes and three new potential genetic causes of human infertility.
evidence: This is based on whole exome sequencing analysis of infertile men and functional validation across species, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transcriptomes tend to cluster by tissue type rather than by species.
source: The fact that transcriptomes tend to cluster by tissue type rather than by species (Merkin et al., 2012) clearly indicates that gene expression identity can be maintained across many million years of evolutionary divergence.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Merkin et al., 2012.

claim: Gene expression identity can be maintained across many million years of evolutionary divergence.
source: The fact that transcriptomes tend to cluster by tissue type rather than by species (Merkin et al., 2012) clearly indicates that gene expression identity can be maintained across many million years of evolutionary divergence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transcriptomes cluster by tissue type rather than species.

claim: Eukaryotic biological processes are modular, with macromolecular complexes built by adding younger components to a core block of ancient subunits.
source: This echoes the modular nature of eukaryotic biological processes, whose intervening macromolecular complexes are typically built by the addition of younger components to a core block of ancient subunits (Wan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wan et al., 2015.

claim: The emergence of germ cells is considered one of the first cell type specializations in metazoan history.
source: The emergence of germ cells is considered one of the first cell type specializations in metazoan history (Arendt, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arendt, 2008.

claim: The capability to undergo both sexual reproduction and gametogenesis were already present in the unicellular ancestor of all Metazoa.
source: Since the capability to undergo both sexual reproduction and gametogenesis were already present in the unicellular ancestor of all Metazoa (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017), the split between germ line and soma presumably provided early multicellular organisms increased robustness against mutations while minimizing genetic conflict between different cell lineages (Extavour, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017.

claim: Reproductive protein genes are some of the most rapidly evolving across the tree of life.
source: Yet, reproductive protein genes are some of the most rapidly evolving across the tree of life (Swanson and Vacquier, 2002), leading to substantial variation in male reproductive tissues even between closely related species (Ramm et al., 2014; Fitzpatrick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Swanson and Vacquier, 2002; Ramm et al., 2014; and Fitzpatrick et al., 2022.

claim: Variation in male reproductive tissues can be mainly traced back to rapid evolutionary changes in gene expression in the testis.
source: At the molecular level, this variation can be mainly traced back to rapid evolutionary changes in gene expression in the testis (Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019) – likely facilitated by widespread transcriptional leakage in male germ cells (Soumillon et al., 2013) – and to the preferential emergence of new genes in this organ (Kaessmann, 2010), where they often acquire functions in spermatogenesis (Kondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019; Soumillon et al., 2013; Kaessmann, 2010; and Kondo et al., 2017.

claim: Widespread transcriptional leakage in male germ cells likely facilitates rapid evolutionary changes in gene expression in the testis.
source: At the molecular level, this variation can be mainly traced back to rapid evolutionary changes in gene expression in the testis (Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019) – likely facilitated by widespread transcriptional leakage in male germ cells (Soumillon et al., 2013) – and to the preferential emergence of new genes in this organ (Kaessmann, 2010), where they often acquire functions in spermatogenesis (Kondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soumillon et al., 2013.

claim: New genes preferentially emerge in the testis and often acquire functions in spermatogenesis.
source: At the molecular level, this variation can be mainly traced back to rapid evolutionary changes in gene expression in the testis (Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019) – likely facilitated by widespread transcriptional leakage in male germ cells (Soumillon et al., 2013) – and to the preferential emergence of new genes in this organ (Kaessmann, 2010), where they often acquire functions in spermatogenesis (Kondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaessmann, 2010 and Kondo et al., 2017.

claim: Old genes make a substantial contribution to the pollen transcriptome across a wide range of plant species.
source: We have recently observed, in a wide range of plant species, a substantial contribution of old genes to the pollen transcriptome, suggestive of an ancient transcriptional program common to plant male gametes (Julca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Julca et al., 2021.

claim: There are transcriptional similarities between equivalent spermatogenic cell types across mammalian species.
source: Such observation finds parallel in the concept of a metazoan germ line multipotency program (Fierro-Constaín et al., 2017), and is supported by transcriptional similarities between equivalent spermatogenic cell types across mammalian species (Lau et al., 2020; Shami et al., 2020; Murat et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lau et al., 2020; Shami et al., 2020; and Murat et al., 2023.

claim: Male germ cells have a generally more diversified transcriptome than their somatic counterparts.
source: We centered our analysis on three evolutionarily distant gonochoric species with excellent genome annotations – humans, mice, and fruit flies (the last two also being well-established animal models for the functional study of human spermatogenesis) – and observed that, as previously reported (Soumillon et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2020), male germ cells have a generally more diversified transcriptome than their somatic counterparts (as measured by the percentage of the entire genome that each cell type expresses).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis and supported by citations to Soumillon et al., 2013 and Xia et al., 2020.

claim: The increased transcriptome complexity in male germ cells is mainly restricted to extremely permissive minimum average expression cut-offs ranging from >0.01 to >0.5 transcripts per million (TPM).
source: Yet, this increased complexity was mainly restricted to extremely permissive minimum average expression cut-offs ranging from >0.01 to >0.5 transcripts per million (TPM), suggestive of a significant degree of transcriptional noise or other previously hypothesized translation-independent roles for lowly expressed transcripts (Liu and Zhang, 2020).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: On average, metazoan male germ cells tend to express approximately 10,000 genes (9,468±498–12,195±1144, depending on the species).
source: Indeed, the use of a more suitable threshold for protein-coding transcripts (TPM >1; Thul et al., 2017) revealed that, on average, metazoan male germ cells tend to express approximately 10,000 genes (9,468±498–12,195±1144, depending on the species), corresponding to half of the entire protein-coding genome (48.0–67.9%; Figure 1b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis using TPM >1 threshold, as shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The majority (65.2 to 70.3%) of genes expressed in male germ cells mapped to the oldest-ranking phylostrata containing orthogroups common to all Metazoa.
source: Despite the rapid divergence typically associated with reproduction-related genes, we found that the majority (65.2 to 70.3%) of genes expressed in male germ cells mapped to the oldest-ranking phylostrata containing orthogroups common to all Metazoa, henceforth referred to as deeply conserved genes (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on phylostratigraphy analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The percentage of deeply conserved genes in male germ cells was not significantly different from that recorded in the transcriptome of somatic cell types.
source: Indeed, in all three tested species, this percentage was not significantly different from that recorded in the transcriptome of the somatic cell types (also at a threshold of TPM >1).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The fraction of deeply conserved genes that were ubiquitously expressed varied from 49.7 to 63.4%.
source: The fraction of deeply conserved genes that were ubiquitously expressed (proxy to their involvement in cellular housekeeping processes) varied from 49.7 to 63.4% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: Almost half of all deeply conserved genes expressed by male germ cells are involved in more specific roles than just the maintenance of basal cellular functions.
source: This strongly suggests that almost half of all deeply conserved genes expressed by male germ cells are involved in more specific roles than just the maintenance of basal cellular functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 49.7-63.4% of deeply conserved genes are ubiquitously expressed.

claim: Meiotic and pre-meiotic cells across all three tested species had lower TAIs than post-meiotic cells, indicative of older transcriptomes.
source: As recently reported in mammalian spermatogenesis (Murat et al., 2023), meiotic and pre-meiotic cells across all three tested species had lower TAIs than post-meiotic cells, indicative of older transcriptomes.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome age index analysis shown in Figure 1e and supported by citation to Murat et al., 2023.

claim: The male germ cell transcriptome has an old evolutionary origin that is tempered by the increased expression of younger genes at later developmental stages.
source: Collectively, we observed that, both in vertebrates and invertebrates, the male germ cell transcriptome has an old evolutionary origin that is tempered by the increased expression of younger genes at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is based on phylostratigraphy and TAI analysis shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: Deeply conserved genes in the spermatocyte PPI networks were significantly more connected than their non-conserved counterparts.
source: Similarly to what we observed in enterocytes, deeply conserved genes in the spermatocyte PPI networks were significantly more connected than their non-conserved counterparts (higher degree centrality), and their interactors were themselves more connected than those of non-conserved genes (higher page rank, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for the two analyses; Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on network analysis shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Machine learning classifiers can reliably predict if a gene was conserved just based on spermatocyte network features.
source: They were still salient enough for machine learning classifiers to predict reliably if a gene was conserved just based on spermatocyte network features. More specifically, using a Random Forest classifier, the AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) score was 0.74, 0.75, and 0.82 in the human, mouse, and fruit fly spermatocyte datasets, respectively (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is based on machine learning analysis shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The orthoBackbone represents less than 3% of all functional interactions (edges) in the spermatocyte PPI networks.
source: We observed that the orthoBackbone drastically reduced the size of the spermatocyte PPI networks, retaining only 1.7 to 2.7% of all edges, depending on the species (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on orthoBackbone analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The orthoBackbone contained 70% of all deeply conserved genes in the network.
source: This almost residual fraction of edges nevertheless contained 70% of all deeply conserved genes in the network (Figure 2c and Supplementary file 2), further illustrating that strong functional relationships between deeply conserved genes are also maintained in the male germ line.
evidence: This is based on orthoBackbone analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: orthoBackbone genes were preferentially involved in gene expression and protein regulation.
source: GO term enrichment analysis for biological processes revealed that orthoBackbone genes were preferentially involved in gene expression and protein regulation, in contrast with the other (not retained) conserved genes that were mainly associated with cell signaling pathways (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a modest overlap between the spermatocyte and enterocyte orthoBackbones, with just 16.2% to 18.0% of common edges depending on the species.
source: We noted a modest overlap between both subnetworks, with just 16.2% to 18.0% of common edges depending on the species (against background expectations of 33.6 to 61.5%, based on Jaccard similarity index scores between the PPI networks of both cell types; Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This is based on network comparison analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: A subset of 79 functional interactions between 104 human genes likely represents a core component of the conserved genetic program of spermatogenesis.
source: Based on its conservation in the orthoBackbone of evolutionarily distant species and on the significant spermatogenic role of the intervening genes, we posit that this subnetwork of 79 functional interactions involving 104 genes likely represents a core component of the conserved genetic program of spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is based on orthoBackbone analysis and GO term filtering shown in Figure 2e.

claim: A total of 250 (27.2%) of the 920 conserved transcriptional burst genes were essential for male fertility.
source: Of these, a total of 250 (27.2%) were essential for male fertility, as their silencing resulted, upon mating with wildtype females, in egg hatching rates below the cut-off of 75% (>2 standard deviations of the mean observed in negative controls: 91.6 ± 8.5%; Figure 2g).
evidence: This is based on in vivo RNAi screening in Drosophila shown in Figure 2g.

claim: 76.0% of the hits (190 out of 250) were part of the orthoBackbone.
source: We observed that 76.0% of the hits (190 out of 250) were part of the orthoBackbone, compared with 60.0% (402 out of 670) in genes without any obvious effect on male reproductive fitness upon silencing, with this difference being statistically significant (two-sided Fisher's exact test p<0.0001).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNAi screen results with orthoBackbone membership.

claim: 161 (64.4%) of all hits had never been previously associated with male reproduction in any species.
source: By exploring publicly available information (see Materials and methods), we determined that 161 (64.4%) of all hits had never been previously associated with male reproduction in any species (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is based on literature review and database searches shown in Figure 2i.

claim: At least 43.5% of the mitosis-to-meiosis transcriptional burst is required for a diverse range of germ cell functions.
source: Overall, by merging our results with previously published data we conclude that at least 43.5% of the mitosis-to-meiosis transcriptional burst (our 250 hits +150 previously reported male fertility genes that gave a negative result in our assay) is required for a diverse range of germ cell functions.
evidence: This is based on combining RNAi screen results with previously published data.

claim: The homozygous loss of function variant c.556_565del;p.(Thr186GlyfsTer119) in RNF113B leads to the abrogation of the protein's two functional domains and to its truncation.
source: This frameshift variant c.556_565del;p.(Thr186GlyfsTer119) leads to the abrogation of the protein's two functional domains (a C3H1-type zinc finger and a RING finger) and to its truncation (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis and protein structure prediction shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The identified man (M1911) shared the homozygous state of the RNF113B LoF variant with his equally infertile brother, but not with his fertile heterozygous brother.
source: The identified man (M1911) is part of a consanguineous family of Middle-Eastern ancestry and shared the homozygous state of the RNF113B LoF variant with his equally infertile brother, but not with his fertile heterozygous brother (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on segregation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c.

claim: The testicular biopsy of M1911 revealed an equivalent meiotic arrest phenotype to that observed in dRNF113-silenced fruit flies.
source: Remarkably, the results from the testicular biopsy of M1911 revealed an equivalent meiotic arrest phenotype to that observed in dRNF113-silenced fruit flies.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3b-c.

claim: Spermatocytes were the most advanced cell stage observed in 89.0% of all assessed human seminiferous tubules in M1911 (vs. 9% in controls).
source: Indeed, spermatocytes were, by far, the predominant cell type in the male gonads of both species: they were the most advanced cell stage observed in 89.0% of all assessed human seminiferous tubules (vs. 9% in controls) and occupied an average of 64.1% of the entire testis area in fruit flies (vs. 12.3% in controls; Figure 3b–c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is based on histological quantification shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Male homozygous Rnf113a2KO/KO mice were sterile and had visibly smaller testes that were largely devoid of germ cells.
source: When compared to wildtype littermates, male homozygous Rnf113a2KO/KO mice were sterile and had visibly smaller testes that were largely devoid of germ cells (SCO: Sertoli cell-only phenotype) except for the rare presence of spermatogonia and spermatocytes (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is based on fertility testing and histological analysis shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–f.

claim: Human RNF113B is predominantly expressed at meiotic entry, peaking at the diplotene stage of prophase I.
source: By analyzing our recently published single-cell RNA-Seq dataset of normal human spermatogenesis (Di Persio et al., 2021), we observed that RNF113B was predominantly expressed at the mitosis-to-meiosis transcriptional burst, peaking at the diplotene stage of prophase I (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The nuclear levels of the fruit fly dRNF113 protein increase at meiotic entry.
source: This mirrored the protein localization pattern of fruit fly dRNF113, characterized by a substantial nuclear accumulation in primary spermatocytes (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The analysis of M1911's testicular transcriptome via RNA-Seq revealed the deregulation of 21.7% of all expressed genes.
source: Consistent with their role in gene expression, the analysis of M1911's testicular transcriptome via RNA-Seq revealed the deregulation of 21.7% of all expressed genes (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: 30.0% of the spermatocyte orthoBackbone network edges were disrupted in M1911's testicular transcriptome.
source: Notably, the deregulation detected in M1911's testicular transcriptome had a clear impact on the spermatocyte orthoBackbone, with 30.0% of its network edges being disrupted (i.e. containing at least one deregulated gene).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis and orthoBackbone mapping shown in Figure 3g.

claim: 20.3% of the fruit fly testicular transcriptome was deregulated in the dRNF113 RNAi, resulting in the disruption of 26.3% of the orthoBackbone.
source: A similar effect was patent in the dRNF113 RNAi, with 20.3% of the fruit fly testicular transcriptome being deregulated, resulting in the disruption of 26.3% of the orthoBackbone (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: The silencing of Prp19 had a lower effect on the orthoBackbone with 15.2% of disrupted edges, despite a similar meiotic arrest phenotype.
source: For comparison, the silencing of Prp19, another transcriptional burst gene and spliceosomal component that RNF113 proteins associate to Gatti da Silva et al., 2019, had a lower effect on the orthoBackbone with 15.2% of disrupted edges (significantly lower than in the dRNF113 RNAi; two-sided Fisher's exact test P<0.0001), despite a similar meiotic arrest phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-d).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis and comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-d.

claim: 38.0% (30 out of 79) of the functional interactions that define the core component of the conserved genetic program of spermatogenesis were disrupted in M1911.
source: Indeed, we noted that 38.0% (30 out of 79) of the functional interactions that define our previously identified core component of the conserved genetic program of spermatogenesis were disrupted in M1911 (i.e. these interactions contained at least one differentially expressed gene; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis and orthoBackbone mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: 19.2% (20 out of 104) of the core spermatogenic program gene subset was found to be downregulated in M1911, compared with 10.0% (1685 out of 16,824) of downregulated genes in the testicular transcriptome.
source: In particular, we observed that 19.2% (20 out of 104) of this gene subset was found to be downregulated, compared with 10.0% (1685 out of 16,824) of downregulated genes in the testicular transcriptome of M1911, with this difference being statistically significant (two-sided Fisher's exact test P=0.0046; Figure 3g).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: 61 conserved human genes were similarly downregulated in both M1911 and the dRNF113 RNAi.
source: By defining the overlap between differentially expressed orthoBackbone genes in the testicular transcriptome of M1911 and of the dRNF113 RNAi, we identified 61 conserved human genes that were similarly downregulated in both species.
evidence: This is based on comparative differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Of the 61 genes similarly downregulated in M1911 and dRNF113 RNAi, 27 had already been linked to male germ cell defects in different species.
source: Of the 61 genes, 27 had already been linked to male germ cell defects in different species: four were clinically validated male infertility genes (CDC14A, CFAP91, DNAI1 and DNAI2), and the other 23 had been previously reported in animal models (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on literature review and database searches.

claim: Two new human male infertility candidate genes were identified: HSPA2 and KPNA2.
source: Filtering these exomes for LoF variants in the 27 selected orthoBackbone genes revealed two new human male infertility candidate genes: HSPA2 and KPNA2.
evidence: This is based on whole exome sequencing analysis of the MERGE cohort.

claim: The mouse and fruit fly HSPA2 homologs (Hspa2 and Hsc70-1 to Hsc70-5, respectively) are required for meiotic progression past the primary spermatocyte stage.
source: HSP70 members are involved in cellular proteostasis from bacteria to human, with the mouse and fruit fly HSPA2 homologs (Hspa2 and Hsc70-1 to Hsc70-5, respectively) being required for meiotic progression past the primary spermatocyte stage (Eddy, 1999; Azuma et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eddy, 1999 and Azuma et al., 2021.

claim: The silencing of Hsc70-1 in the fruit fly testis resulted in an equivalent meiotic arrest to that of dRNF113.
source: Indeed, we observed that the silencing of Hsc70-1 in the fruit fly testis, also with the bam-GAL4 driver, resulted in an equivalent meiotic arrest to that of dRNF113, strongly suggesting that the misexpression of this chaperone is a central element of the latter phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 5a–b).
evidence: This is based on in vivo RNAi and histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5a–b.

claim: Two different heterozygous LoF variants in HSPA2 were detected in the male infertility cohort.
source: Two different heterozygous LoF variants were detected in our male infertility cohort, with this gene having a predicted autosomal-dominant inheritance (Figure 3—figure supplement 5c–f and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on whole exome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5c–f.

claim: The first HSPA2 variant, detected in individual M1678, is the early stop-gain variant c.175C>T;p.(Gln59Ter) that truncates more than 90% of the protein.
source: The first variant, detected in individual M1678, is the early stop-gain variant c.175C>T;p.(Gln59Ter) that truncates more than 90% of the protein, likely leading to nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis.

claim: The second HSPA2 variant, identified in individual M2190, is the frameshift variant c.1806dup;p.(Glu603ArgfsTer81) which affects the distal end of the protein's nucleotide-binding domain.
source: The second, identified in individual M2190, is the frameshift variant c.1806dup;p.(Glu603ArgfsTer81) which affects the distal end of the protein's nucleotide-binding domain.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis.

claim: Histopathological analysis of M2190's testicular tissue revealed a SCO phenotype in 259 assessed seminiferous tubules.
source: Histopathological analysis of M2190's testicular tissue revealed a SCO phenotype in 259 assessed seminiferous tubules, a likely aggravation of the extensive cell death accompanied by tubule vacuolization reported in Hspa2 mutant mice (Dix et al., 1996; Figure 3j).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The mouse ortholog of KPNA2 (Kpna2) is required for the nuclear accumulation of Hop2.
source: Its mouse ortholog (Kpna2) is required for the nuclear accumulation of Hop2 (Ly-Huynh et al., 2011), a conserved regulator of meiotic progression from yeast to mammals (Leu et al., 1998; Petukhova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ly-Huynh et al., 2011; Leu et al., 1998; and Petukhova et al., 2003.

claim: Drosophila importin alpha 2 (dKPNA2) is required for post-meiotic development.
source: Yet, Drosophila importin alpha 2 (dKPNA2, also known as Pendulin) is required for post-meiotic development (Mason et al., 2002), with its silencing specifically at meiotic entry being associated with aborted spermiogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on in vivo RNAi and histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6a–b, and supported by citation to Mason et al., 2002.

claim: Two heterozygous KPNA2 LoF variants were detected in the cohort of infertile men.
source: We detected two heterozygous KPNA2 LoF variants in our cohort of infertile men, with this gene also having a predicted autosomal-dominant inheritance (Figure 3—figure supplement 6c–g and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on whole exome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6c–g.

claim: The splice-site variant (c.667–2A>G;p.?) in individual M1645 is predicted to disrupt the correct splicing of intron 6 due to the loss of an acceptor site.
source: The splice-site variant (c.667–2A>G;p.?) in individual M1645 is predicted to disrupt the correct splicing of intron 6 due to the loss of an acceptor site.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis.

claim: Segregation analysis revealed the de novo occurrence of the KPNA2 variant in M1645.
source: Segregation analysis revealed the de novo occurrence of this variant, strongly supporting both its pathogenicity and our recent results, pointing to the important contribution of heterozygous de novo mutations to male infertility (Oud et al., 2022; Wyrwoll et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on segregation analysis and supported by citations to Oud et al., 2022 and Wyrwoll et al., 2023.

claim: The other KPNA2 LoF variant, in individual M2098, is the frameshift variant c.1158_1161del;p.(Ser387ArgfsTer14) which affects 27% of the protein.
source: The other KPNA2 LoF variant, in individual M2098, is the frameshift variant c.1158_1161del;p.(Ser387ArgfsTer14) which affects 27% of the protein, including its minor nuclear localization signal binding site.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis.

claim: Both HSPA2 and KPNA2 can represent haploinsufficient genes and/or have autosomal dominant inheritance, with the evidence being stronger for KPNA2.
source: Based on three in silico prediction tools (Materials and methods), both HSPA2 and KPNA2 can represent haploinsufficient genes and/or have autosomal dominant inheritance, with the evidence being stronger for KPNA2.
evidence: This is based on in silico prediction analysis described in Materials and methods.

claim: KPNA2 is a strong novel autosomal-dominant candidate gene.
source: Together with the identified de novo occurrence of one of its LoF variants, this makes KPNA2 a strong novel autosomal-dominant candidate gene while more data is still needed before drawing similar conclusions on HSPA2.
evidence: This is based on the combination of de novo occurrence, in silico predictions, and functional data.

claim: Deeply conserved genes play a prominent role in male germ cell regulation.
source: Overall, we show that deeply conserved genes play a prominent role in male germ cell regulation and that the disruption of this ancient genetic program leads to human reproductive disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the presented data.

claim: The disruption of the ancient genetic program of male germ cells leads to human reproductive disease.
source: Overall, we show that deeply conserved genes play a prominent role in male germ cell regulation and that the disruption of this ancient genetic program leads to human reproductive disease.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the identification of RNF113B, HSPA2, and KPNA2 as causes of human infertility.

claim: The transcriptional identity of metazoan male germ cells is built around a relatively small network of deeply conserved gene interactions with an overarching functional impact.
source: We propose that the transcriptional identity of metazoan male germ cells is built around a relatively small network of deeply conserved gene interactions with an overarching functional impact.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the orthoBackbone analysis and functional screening results.

claim: The existence of a shared genetic identity in metazoan spermatocytes can be regarded as a ramification of an ancestral multipotency program already present in germ line precursor cells.
source: The existence of a shared genetic identity in metazoan spermatocytes can be regarded as a ramification of an ancestral multipotency program already present in germ line precursor cells (Fierro-Constaín et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation supported by citation to Fierro-Constaín et al., 2017.

claim: Male infertility affects up to 12% of all men.
source: Since male infertility affects up to 12% of all men (Agarwal et al., 2015), addressing such knowledge gap is an issue of clear medical importance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2015.

claim: Male infertility has a low causative diagnostic yield (typically just 30%).
source: This contributes to a low causative diagnostic yield (typically just 30%), and to a paucity of clinically validated genes (currently just 104, in contrast with the more than 700 already associated with other clinical disorders such as intellectual disability [Houston et al., 2021; Vissers et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Houston et al., 2021 and Vissers et al., 2016.

claim: There are currently just 104 clinically validated male infertility genes.
source: This contributes to a low causative diagnostic yield (typically just 30%), and to a paucity of clinically validated genes (currently just 104, in contrast with the more than 700 already associated with other clinical disorders such as intellectual disability [Houston et al., 2021; Vissers et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Houston et al., 2021 and Vissers et al., 2016.
